lesson.title: The Bridge: How Differentiation and Integration Undo Each Other
lesson.summary: The fundamental theorem of calculus reveals that the two seemingly separate ideas of slope and area are inverse processes of each other, replacing the brute force limit of a Riemann sum with a fast shortcut built from antiderivatives.
lesson.body:
Every definite integral so far in this sequence has been evaluated the hard way: build a Riemann sum, find a closed formula for it in terms of n, then take a limit. That works for simple functions like x or x^2, but the algebra gets brutal fast, and for many functions there is no tidy closed formula for the sum at all. The fundamental theorem of calculus is the discovery that rescues this situation, and it does so by connecting the definite integral to something apparently unrelated: the antiderivative, a function whose derivative gives back the original integrand.

The theorem comes in two parts, and both rest on the same underlying fact, that differentiation and integration are inverse operations of one another. Part one says that if you build a new function F(x) by accumulating f from a fixed starting point a up to a variable point x, meaning F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is itself differentiable and F'(x) = f(x). In other words, differentiating an accumulation function just gives back the function you were accumulating. Part two says that if F is any antiderivative of f at all, meaning F'(x) = f(x) everywhere on [a, b], then the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals F(b) minus F(a). Together these say that computing a definite integral, an inherently infinite limiting process built from a sum, can be reduced to finding one antiderivative and evaluating it at two points.

Here is a worked example that shows both directions using the same function, f(t) = 2t. For part one's direction, build F(x) = the integral from 0 to x of 2t dt. Geometrically this is the area of a triangle with base x and height 2x (since f(x) = 2x), so F(x) = 1/2 times x times 2x = x^2. Differentiating gives F'(x) = 2x, which is exactly f(x) again, confirming part one. For part two's direction, evaluate the integral from 1 to 3 of 2t dt using this same F: F(3) - F(1) = 9 - 1 = 8. Check it geometrically as a trapezoid with parallel sides f(1) = 2 and f(3) = 6 and width 2: (2 + 6)/2 times 2 = 8, matching exactly. One antiderivative, x^2, handled both the differentiation direction and the evaluation direction without a single Riemann sum in sight.

This is why the fundamental theorem earns its name: it is the hinge connecting two branches of calculus that, up to this point, looked like they were about completely different things, tangent line slopes on one side and areas under curves on the other. It turns out the limit defining a derivative and the limit defining a definite integral are two views of the same underlying structure. The next two chapters take each half of this theorem in turn and dig into exactly why it works, starting with the differentiation direction.
